title: America's Treasury Secretary Threatens Allies with Divine Wrath, Proving He Has No Cards
dek: Treasury Secretary Bessent portrays the US as an angry god, demanding allies submit as if to Pascal's wager. Farrell sees through the editorial: the louder the threat, the more it proves the US lacks the means to follow through, and allies are already hedging.
why: A contrarian reading of a seemingly tough Treasury editorial: theological bluster rarely translates into action, and understanding this helps predict allies' true leverage in trade negotiations.
who: Decision-makers in cross-border business, investors watching dollar assets and tariff risks, and policy researchers trying to gauge whether allies will cave.
skip: Skip the first 4 minutes of intro and subscription pitch; start directly with Carney's speech and Bessent's editorial.

points.h: The Treasury chief casts America as an angry god
points.body: In his Financial Times editorial on 'economic D-Day,' Bessent frames allies' choice as a Pascal's wager. Farrell's read: he's really saying you must treat the US as God and appease this wrathful deity by all means, or it will strike you with lightning. Farrell likens it to a 17th-century Puritan sermon, retitled 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God,' with the sinners being the rest of the world. The problem: such pulpit-thumping usually signals a pastor losing his congregation, not strength.

points.h: The louder the shout, the softer the stick
points.body: Roosevelt's maxim was 'speak softly and carry a big stick.' Farrell says Bessent reverses it: speak bigly and carry a soft stick. The real test is China—the country most capable of supporting Iran—and Bessent avoids answering whether the US would dare turn its wrath on China if it keeps buying Iranian oil. Farrell believes markets and nations are betting 'no.' So the editorial reads as an empty threat: the more absolute the language, the more it looks like bluffing on an empty table.

points.h: Flexible realism is no strategy at all
points.body: Explaining White House behavior as 'flexible realism' is just draping a cloth over chaos. Farrell says the term, unpacked, means only: the US does whatever it wants, and other countries should adapt. What actually drives the White House is not strategy but a scramble for attention, like Cosimo de' Medici making everyone revolve around him—but Trump does 'a stupid version': to be the center of attention, he'll make decisions that are idiotic in both the short and long term. Other countries respond by cutting losses rather than doubling down.

Federalist No. 10's answer was 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition': let each person's drive for power cancel the others, grinding toward a near-public-interest equilibrium. Farrell says that mechanism is dismantled from two ends. One is the Republican Party: internal dissent has nearly vanished; senators won't openly block even if they object; same-party control of all three branches short-circuits checks. The other is the federal bureaucracy: the Supreme Court embraces the unitary executive theory, inspectors general are fired or cowed, and career civil servants are converted to at-will employees. An utterly incompetent person at the top magnifies errors into national madness.

points.h: Rebuilding US institutions requires learning to experiment
points.body: Farrell doesn't think institutions can return to the old consensus of the early 1990s to 2015, but he also doesn't see the US doomed to disaster. His hopeful example is New York Mayor Mamdani's experiment: building feedback loops between city government and the public, turning people's real troubles into policy, and using social media to show 'I'm listening and acting.' He explicitly links this to Roosevelt's 'bold, persistent experimentation': keep what works, discard what doesn't. The open question is whether America's media and political system can tolerate a politician openly saying 'this path failed, let's try another'—without that tolerance, experiments won't go far.

points.h: The more flexible, the less anyone takes you seriously
points.body: The biggest problem with flexible realism is that it destroys an asset that erodes with caprice—credibility. Farrell cites Nobel laureate Thomas Schelling: a nation's most important assets include credibility; promises and threats that can be honored are what actually work in negotiation. If you change your mind at will, if yesterday's solemn threat vanishes tomorrow, at some point no one takes you seriously. Farrell sees the US in that state today: other nations still fear its capacity to harm but no longer believe in its long-term capacity to act. His image: a drunk grandfather with a shotgun—everyone just humors him so he doesn't fire.

points.h: America is smashing its own web with a sledgehammer
points.body: In 'Underground Empire,' Farrell and Newman's core point: globalization is a web of interdependence—supply chains stitch together dozens of countries and thousands of suppliers, and dollar clearing is the nervous system. The US built this system and reserved a 'house advantage,' threatening to cut off access to discipline others. The Trump administration isn't delicately dismantling the web; it's swinging a sledgehammer at random parts. Farrell's direction is clear: full decoupling would be a disaster; the answer isn't independence but making interdependence resilient, while major powers relearn 'restraint.'

points.h: A rare-earth card punctures the myth of invincibility
points.body: On last year's 'Liberation Day,' Bessent publicly said the US held all the aces and China had none. Weeks later, China played its rare-earth and critical-minerals card, and the US suddenly realized it held a busted flush—a hand that looked fierce but never materialized. Farrell sees this as the moment that sobered Washington; since then, Marco Rubio and others have shown awareness that China can materially hurt the US economy. The US and China now live in a fragile balance where each knows 'I can hurt you badly,' but they haven't yet sat down to turn that balance into more stable rules.
